Here's a full breakdown of **looting** in Frosthaven:

---

## The *Loot* Ability

> "*Loot* X" is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 111)*

---

## Looting Loot Tokens

When a loot token is looted, it is removed from the map. What happens next depends on who looted it:

- **Monsters:** Nothing else happens.
- **Characters:** Draw one card from the **loot deck** (unless it's empty).

---

## The Loot Deck

Each scenario has a custom loot deck built from four types of loot cards:

| Type | Details |
|---|---|
| **Money** 🪙 | 20 cards showing 1–3 coins; converted to gold based on scenario level at end of scenario. |
| **Material Resources** | 8 cards per type (lumber, metal, hide); amount varies by number of characters. |
| **Herb Resources** | 2 cards per type (arrowvine, axenut, corpsecap, flamefruit, rockroot, snowthistle); provides 1 herb each. |
| **Random Item** | 1 card; provides a random item drawn from the random item deck. Gained **immediately** when looted. |

Money and resources are **not gained until the end of the scenario**. Random items are gained immediately and can be used for the rest of the scenario even if it puts the character over the item limit for that type.

*(Rulebook, passage 67)*

---

## Looting Treasure Tiles

When a **treasure tile** is looted, it is removed from the map. **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.** If the treasure is a numbered treasure, reference the Treasure Index and apply the effect — only the looting character gains the reward (unless it is a random item blueprint or random scenario).

*(Rulebook, passages 111–112)*

Here's how recommended scenario level works in Frosthaven:

## Recommended Scenario Level

> At recommended difficulty, the scenario level is equal to the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up).

**Formula:** `Average Character Level ÷ 2 (rounded up)`

**Example:** If all characters are level 2, the average (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is still level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase.

---

### Adjusting Difficulty

The recommended level is just a starting point. At the start of any scenario, you can set the scenario level to **any number from 0–7**:
- **Decrease** it if your party is struggling.
- **Increase** it to keep the game challenging as your party grows stronger.

---

### What Scenario Level Affects

| Scenario Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monster Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| Gold Conversion | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Trap Damage | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| Hazardous Terrain | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 |
| Bonus Experience | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 |

---

### Special Cases

- **Solo Mode:** Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 and rounding up, to account for easier coordination. *(e.g., three level 4 characters = level 2 normally, but level 3 in solo mode)*
- **Open Information variant:** Use the same solo mode formula, for the same reason.

*(Rulebook, passages 67–68 and 203)*

Here's how *advantage* works with attack modifier cards in Frosthaven, based on the rulebook:

---

## Advantage — Drawing Two Modifiers

When an attack has *advantage*, the attacker **draws two modifier cards** and gets to choose which one to use:

- **Monsters** always use the better one.
- **Characters** may use either one (even the worse one, if desired).

---

## Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

If the **first card drawn** is a *rolling modifier*, the process extends:

1. Keep drawing cards one at a time until you hit a **non-rolling modifier**.
2. Then draw **one more** card, ignoring any rolling icon on it.
3. You now compare those **last two** cards (the first non-rolling one and the one after it).
4. You **keep all the initial rolling modifiers** and use whichever of those last two you choose (for a character) or the better one (for a monster).

If the **second card** (not the first) is a rolling modifier, its rolling icon is **still ignored**.

---

## Ambiguity

When it's unclear which modifier is "better" or "worse" (e.g., one grants an elemental infusion or a condition instead of a numeric bonus), any non-numeric effect is treated as having a **positive but undefined value**. In cases of true ambiguity, the attacker **must use the first card drawn**.

---

## Advantage + Disadvantage Cancel Out

> "An attack cannot gain multiple instances of advantage or disadvantage. If an attack has both advantage and disadvantage, it is considered to have neither."

---

## Ranged Attacks on Adjacent Enemies

Any ranged attack targeting an **adjacent enemy** automatically gains *disadvantage*, regardless of other sources of *advantage*.

---

*Source: Frosthaven Rulebook, passages 96–97*

## Long Rests in Frosthaven

**When to declare:** During the **Card Selection** step, instead of selecting two ability cards to play, a character may declare a long rest — but only if they have **at least two cards in their discard pile**. (Rulebook, passage 72)

**Initiative:** A character who declares a long rest acts on **initiative 99** and takes no other turn that round. (Rulebook, passage 72)

**What happens on your long rest turn (in order):**

1. **Lose one card of your choice** from your discard pile, then return all remaining discard pile cards to your hand. *(Mandatory)*
2. **Heal 2, self.** *(Optional)*
3. **Recover all spent items.** Items can even be used during the same turn they are recovered. *(Optional)*

(Rulebook, passage 125)

---

**Key differences from a short rest:**
- A short rest happens at the **End of Round** step and loses a **random** card (with a damage-pay option to redraw once). A long rest happens during **Card Selection**, lets you choose which card to lose, heals you, and recovers items — at the cost of your entire turn.

Great question — this is addressed directly by both the Rulebook and the official FAQ. Here's how it plays out:

## The Monster Stays Put and Attacks at Disadvantage

The monster will **not** move through the traps. It will remain adjacent to you and perform its ranged attack at *disadvantage*.

Here's the reasoning from the rules:

**1. Monsters prefer safe paths over any path through negative hexes (traps), even much longer ones.**

> "A monster's first focus priority is to choose a hex from which they can attack an enemy, using the least possible movement, preferring 'safe' paths of any length over any paths with negative hexes. They will only choose a path with one or more negative hexes if it's the only way to attack any enemy, **ever**, looking at the current state of the board, pretending the monster has infinite movement."

— *FAQ, passage 40*

Since the monster can already attack you from where it stands (just at *disadvantage*), entering a trap to avoid that *disadvantage* is **not** required to attack "at all." The safe option (staying put and attacking at *disadvantage*) exists, so the monster takes it.

**2. A monster with a ranged attack will try to move away from an adjacent target to avoid disadvantage — but only if it can do so without entering a negative hex.**

> "If the monster would lose disadvantage by moving away from its focus, if it can do so with its current movement, and if it **can do so without entering a negative hex**, it will."

— *FAQ, passage 39*

Moving through the traps is entering a negative hex, so the monster will not do it just to shed *disadvantage*.

**3. The Rulebook confirms the general preference:**

> "When a monster performs a ranged attack on an adjacent target, it first moves away from that target if possible, so that the attack does not have disadvantage."

— *Rulebook, passage 177*

The key word is "if possible" — and the FAQ clarifies that moving through traps does not count as a valid "possible" option for this purpose.

---

**Bottom line:** The monster stays where it is, attacks you at *disadvantage*, and does **not** walk through the traps to get a clean shot.

---

## The *Loot* Ability

> **"Loot X"** is an ability that allows a figure to loot all money tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles. If there are no money tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range, the ability cannot be performed.

*(Rulebook, passage 132)*

---

## End-of-Turn Looting

> Characters must loot any money tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex **at the end of their turn**. No figures besides characters perform end-of-turn looting.

- This happens at the **end of the turn**, not at the end of each movement.
- Monsters and summons do **not** perform end-of-turn looting.

*(Rulebook, passages 156 & 290)*

---

## Looting Money Tokens

- When a money token is looted, it is **removed from the map**.
- If a **monster** loots it, nothing else happens.
- If a **character** loots it, they place the token on their character mat.

*(Rulebook, passage 133)*

---

## Looting Treasure Tiles

- When a treasure tile is looted, it is **removed from the map**.
- **Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.**
- If the looted treasure is a **numbered treasure**, reference its number in the Treasure Index and apply the effect.
- Only the looting character gains the reward (unless it is a random item design or random scenario).
- If a character gains a copy of an item they already own, they must **give it to another character or sell it immediately**.

*(Rulebook, passage 133)*

---

## Monster Loot Abilities

Some monsters have explicit loot abilities on their ability cards. In those cases:
- The monster loots all money tokens within the specified range, removing them from the map.
- These money tokens are **not dropped** by the monster when it dies.
- Monsters are still **unable to loot treasure tiles**.

*(Rulebook, passage 182)*

Here's how the recommended scenario level is calculated in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

> **Recommended Scenario Level = Average Character Level ÷ 2 (rounded up)**

For example, if all characters are level 2, the average (2) ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario is level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase to 2.

**A few important notes:**

- You can set the scenario level to **any value from 0–7** at the start of a scenario — the recommended level is just a starting point.
- The scenario level affects: **monster level, gold conversion, trap damage, hazardous terrain damage, and bonus experience** (see the chart below).

| Scenario Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monster Level | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
| Gold Conversion | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| Trap Damage | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
| Hazardous Terrain | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 4 |
| Bonus Experience | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 18 |

---

**Special cases:**

- **Solo mode:** Add 1 to the average character level *before* dividing by 2 (rounded up), to account for the reduced uncertainty of controlling multiple characters yourself. E.g., three level-4 characters normally give scenario level 2, but in solo mode it becomes level 3.
- **Open Information variant:** Use the same adjusted formula as solo mode.

Here's how *Advantage* works with attack modifier cards in **Gloomhaven (2nd Edition)**:

---

### Basic Rule

> With **advantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

### Rolling Modifiers with Advantage

If the **first** card drawn is a *rolling modifier*, the process extends:

1. Keep drawing cards one at a time until you draw a non-rolling modifier.
2. Then draw **one more** card — and ignore any rolling icon on that final card.
3. You now have: all the initial rolling modifiers + two non-rolling results to compare.
4. With *advantage*: you apply all the initial rolling modifiers **and** whichever of the last two cards you choose.

### Rolling Modifiers with Disadvantage (for contrast)

> With **disadvantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and always uses the worse one.

- **Characters** get to choose which of the two final cards to use when they have *advantage* — monsters do not get that choice.
- *Advantage* and *disadvantage* only affect the modifier draw, not the base attack value.
- Attack modifier cards are only drawn for attacks, not for other effects that deal damage.
